title: Budget versus actual with a variance flag

docs.syntax: =ROUND((actual-budget)/budget,3) sizes the variance; ABS lets one threshold catch both directions
docs.explain:
Dividing a variance by its budget turns an amount into a share of what was planned. That is what lets one threshold fit every line: 100 over on a 2000 budget is five per cent, and the same 100 over on 300 is a third. ROUND keeps the share at three decimals so two cells can be compared.

The rent line asks for that share directly: 2100 actual against a 2000 budget is 0.05. The second screen turns the same arithmetic into a flag, with the threshold at ten per cent in either direction.

Without ABS the test reads a signed difference, so an underspend never reaches review. Payroll at 4800 against a 5000 budget is four per cent under and would pass unnoticed. Travel at 950 against 800 is the line that does flag, at 18.75 per cent.

errors.text: The budget cell is zero, so the variance has nothing to be divided by.
A budget or actual cell holds text, so the subtraction has no number to work with.
A flag built on the signed difference catches overspends and lets an underspend through, which is what ABS around the difference prevents.

docs.atWork: Turning a budget column and an actual column into a variance a reader can compare across lines.
docs.outcome: Size a variance as a share of budget, then flag it with one threshold both ways.
docs.teaches: a rounded variance share, then an IF over ABS so under- and overspends both flag
docs.dataset: Four budget lines with budget, actual and one answer cell

screens.prompt: In D2, report the actual-vs-budget variance of the first line as a share of its budget, to three decimal places.

hints.syntax: =ROUND((C2-B2)/B2,3): the difference over the budget, to three places.
hints.func-round: The raw ratio runs to a long tail of digits, so it is rounded for reporting.
hints.require-ref: The budget is in B2 and the actual in C2, on the same row.
hints.value: A hundred over two thousand is five per cent, or 0.05.
hints.error: A zero budget leaves the share nothing to measure against, and the cell shows #DIV/0!.

reject.why: the difference is left as an amount rather than a share
a hundred pounds is not five per cent
the subtraction runs the wrong way, giving a negative share
the difference is measured against the actual rather than the budget
the formula reads the second line rather than B2
the difference is divided by zero
the arguments fall outside the parentheses

screens.prompt: In D2, flag the first line review when its variance is more than ten per cent in either direction and ok otherwise.

hints.syntax: =IF(ABS(C2-B2)/B2>0.1,"review","ok"): the absolute share, then the threshold, then two words.
hints.func-if: One branch for a line worth review and one for a line that is fine.
hints.func-abs: An overspend and an underspend both count, so the difference is taken without its sign.
hints.require-ref: The budget is B2 and the actual C2, not the answer column.
hints.value: Five per cent is inside ten, so the first line reads ok.
hints.error: If the test uses the signed difference, the grader reports the flag as wrong for an underspend.

reject.why: the flag is typed rather than decided by the variance
the size of the variance never enters, so any overspend flags
a hundred pounds is compared against a share
the formula reads the second line rather than B2
the difference is divided by zero inside the test
the arguments fall outside the parentheses

seo.title: Budget versus actual with a variance flag
seo.description: A variance divided by its budget lets one threshold fit every line. ABS around the difference catches underspends too, so nothing slips past review.
